resources.string: The time at which the app was first installed.
The time at which the app was last updated.

If the package is installed, it shows the application that installed this package.\nThis identifies which market the package came from, such as Google Play Store.\nIf not, it shows the application who launched APK Checker.
The real full path of the .apk file.\n(It\'s a duplication if red. Because the raw APK is not accessible.)
The name of the .apk file.\n(It\'s a duplication if red. Because the raw APK is not accessible.)
What you see is raw image without scaling.
The size should be 48*48dp according to official documents.
A full Java-language-style package name for the application.\nThe name should be unique.\nOnce an application published, the package name could not be changed.
Line 1 is name according to current language, and line 2 is in English (if exists).
The version number shown to users.
An internal version number.\nThis number is used only to determine whether one version is more recent than another, with higher numbers indicating more recent versions.
The date when the application package was created.\nNotice that, it\'s not always accurate.

An integer designating the minimum API Level required for the application to run.\nThe Android system will prevent the user from installing the application if the system\'s API Level is lower than the value specified in this attribute.
An integer designating the API Level that the application targets.
ABIs supported by this application.\nNotice that, it\'s not always correct.

Android is a privilege-separated operating system, and additional finer-grained security features are provided through a "permission" mechanism that enforces restrictions on the specific operations that a particular process can perform.
"Requested permissions" lists all permissions this application requested.
(The red is permission which is dangerous defined in API 23.
Dangerous permissions cover areas where the app wants data or resources that involve the user's private information, or could potentially affect the user's stored data or the operation of other apps.)
Declares a security permission that can be used to limit access to specific components or features of this or other applications.
A front-door activity in a package.\nIf the value were empty, there would be no the application\'s icon in \"Launcher\".
An activity represents a single screen with a user interface.\nIt is one of the four essential app components for an Android app.\n(The green is activity which is available for use by other apps.)

A service is a component that runs in the background to perform long-running operations or to perform work for remote processes.
A service does not provide a user interface.
It is one of the four essential app components for an Android app.
(The green is service which is available for use by other apps.)
A content provider manages a shared set of app data.\nIt is one of the four essential app components for an Android app.\n(The green is content provider which is available for use by other apps.)

A broadcast receiver is a component that responds to system-wide broadcast announcements.
Many broadcasts originate from the system.
It is one of the four essential app components for an Android app.
(The green is receiver which is available for use by other apps.)

A signing certificate associated with the application package.
All APKs (.apk files) must be signed with a certificate whose private key is held by their developer.
This certificate identifies the author of the application.
"Signatures" shows the following items: CN(first and last name), OU(organizational unit), O(organization), L(city or locality), ST(state or province) and C(country code).
(Red if informal.)
It shows the following items: the name of the algorithm for the certificate signature, the certificates version, hash value of MD5, hash value of SHA1 and hash value of SHA256.
The start of the validity period of the certificate.
The end of the validity period of the certificate.
